title: Solar and wind power in 2026 | City council briefing

slides.name: 2026 briefing

image.alt: Illustration of solar panels and distant wind turbines near a city skyline at dawn

blocks.text: CITY COUNCIL BRIEFING  •  SEPTEMBER 2026
Solar and wind are scaling; ==local readiness determines value==
The latest complete global data are from 2025. Here is what they mean—and do not mean—for a city.

slides.notes: This is a 2026 decision briefing, grounded in the latest completed global year, 2025. Global momentum provides a reason to evaluate options, not proof that any particular city project is viable. We will separate observed generation, new capacity, costs and local implementation questions.

sources.title: Near-700 GW Surge in 2025 Proves Renewable Energy Resilience

slides.name: 2025 capacity additions

blocks.text: 01  /  SCALE
In 2025, ==solar led== another record year for renewables

children.label: Renewables’ share of all power-capacity additions

blocks.text: Global additions, not electricity generated. Source: IRENA, 2026.

slides.notes: IRENA reports 692 GW of renewable capacity added in 2025, reaching 5,149 GW worldwide. Solar and wind additions are subsets of that figure; the 85.6% figure describes all renewables as a share of total power-capacity additions. Capacity added does not tell us how much electricity was generated or when it was available.

sources.title: Near-700 GW Surge in 2025 Proves Renewable Energy Resilience

slides.name: Solar installed capacity trend

blocks.text: 02  /  TRAJECTORY
Global installed solar capacity reached ==2,392 GW== at end-2025

children.caption: Year-end global solar capacity (GW). Source: IRENA, Renewable capacity statistics 2026.

children.title: Read the metric carefully
children.text: This is **installed capacity**, not annual electricity output.

slides.notes: The chart reproduces IRENA's year-end installed solar capacity series for 2021–2025. End-2025 capacity rose from 1,880.396 GW at end-2024 to 2,391.584 GW. Capacity is a stock measured in GW; it should not be equated with generation in TWh.

slides.name: Electricity generation share

blocks.text: 03  /  ELECTRICITY ACTUALLY GENERATED
Solar and wind supplied ==about 17%== of global electricity in 2025

children.label: Solar + wind share of global electricity, 2025

blocks.text: Sources: IEA, Electricity 2026; Ember, Global Electricity Review 2026.

slides.notes: The IEA estimates solar and wind together provided approximately 17% of global generation in 2025 and forecasts a 27% share in 2030; that latter number is a projection, not an observed result. Ember reports a 33.8% 2025 share for all renewables, which includes technologies beyond solar and wind. These figures describe electricity supplied, rather than new installations.

slides.name: Global new-generation costs

blocks.text: 04  /  ECONOMICS
New solar and onshore wind are ==cost-competitive globally==
These are **2025 global weighted-average levelised costs** for new plants—not local bids or all-hour delivered prices.
Source: IRENA, Renewable power generation costs in 2025.

slides.notes: IRENA reports global weighted-average levelised costs of USD 44/MWh for new solar PV, USD 33/MWh for onshore wind and USD 78/MWh for offshore wind commissioned in 2025. More than 90% of utility-scale renewables commissioned that year were cheaper than the cheapest new fossil-fuel alternative in their respective markets, according to IRENA. Council should not substitute these world averages for city-specific bids, grid costs or delivered hourly prices.

slides.name: Grid flexibility requirement

blocks.text: 05  /  SYSTEM DESIGN
The next constraint is ==matching clean output to demand==

blocks.title: Council implication
blocks.text: Evaluate supply **together with** connection needs, storage and demand flexibility.
System-flexibility evidence: IEA, Electricity 2026.

slides.notes: The IEA identifies batteries and flexible demand as means to shift renewable electricity toward periods when demand is higher. The flow is a decision framework rather than a claim that each technology must be built locally or in this exact order. Grid access and operating patterns need examination before procurement or capital commitments.

slides.name: Council next steps

blocks.text: 06  /  DECISION FOR COUNCIL
Commission a ==local options assessment== before choosing projects

items.title: Map local opportunity
items.text: Roofs, land, wind resource and permitting

items.title: Test deliverability
items.text: Grid capacity, hourly demand and flexibility

items.title: Compare real offers
items.text: Local bids, procurement terms and risk

blocks.text: Global results establish momentum—not this city’s resource quality, tariffs or project economics.

slides.notes: The proposed council action is to authorize a scoped, local options assessment rather than select a technology on global averages alone. Assess local resources and permitting, network and hourly operating constraints, then compare actual offers and procurement structures. No city was specified, so this briefing makes no claim about site-level economics or grid availability.
